title: Corruption Claims, Flock Cameras, and Empty Chairs: What the TAMIU Council Debate Revealed Before Early Voting

content:
Two weeks before early voting, candidates for three Laredo City Council seats faced students at Texas A&M International University — and the sharpest exchange of the night was about whether Laredo’s government is corrupt.

The October 6 “Laredo Decides” debate, hosted by TAMIU’s Student Government Association Political Action Committee in the Student Center Ballroom, put the District 2, 3, and 6 contenders through 40-minute sessions each, with audience questions to follow. The Bridge, TAMIU’s student news outlet, covered it on October 15.

The clash

District 3 challenger Michelle Marie Winterroth didn’t mince words: “Laredo is a very corrupt city, and I’ve seen it firsthand,” she said, adding that her “order is to ensure there is no corruption and the right people get the right spots and that there is no favoritism in the work field.”

District 3 incumbent Melissa R. Cigarroa pushed back: “I have not seen it; these are unsupported accusations that have no basis in evidence, and this is not the experience I have had,” she said, defending city staff’s degrees and certifications.

The District 2 matchup — Ricardo Rangel Jr. vs. Daisy Alejandra Campos — and District 6 — incumbent Dr. David Tyler King vs. Ubaldo Granados Jr. — rounded out the night. All three races are on the November 3 ballot, along with Districts I and VI and the mayor’s office.

The technology question

Beyond personalities, the debate surfaced a live policy issue: Flock cameras — the networked license-plate-reader cameras expanding across Texas cities. Politically engaged student Amador Flores III told The Bridge he’s “often wary of too many students or people my age getting involved in politics,” but added, “when it comes to the topic of Flock [cameras], there aren’t enough people involved.” Surveillance policy, it turns out, is one of the issues that can pull young voters off the sidelines — if anyone’s talking to them about it.

The empty chairs

Here’s the uncomfortable part for the organizers: despite a debate designed specifically to energize students, “there was little student turnout,” The Bridge reported. Moderator Emily Esparza said her committee’s goal was for college peers “to show up to the polls with the right amount of confidence and information to make an informed decision.” The information was there. The peers, mostly, were not.

Analysis

The corruption exchange is the tell. Winterroth’s charge is broad and, as Cigarroa correctly noted, unsupported by specific evidence in her remarks — accusations without examples are just rhetoric. But the fact that a council challenger can make that claim to applause-worthy silence rather than instant dismissal says something about public trust at city hall two weeks before voters weigh in. Candidates don’t reach for “corrupt city” framing when the electorate is satisfied.

Meanwhile, the city held its own candidate forums at City Hall earlier this month — Districts I and VI on October 6, Districts III and II on October 7, and the Municipal Court Place 1 forum on October 8 — and the city’s nonpartisan voter campaign is running through Election Day. The stage has been set. Now early voting, which opens today, will show whether Laredo actually shows up.
